Fair call. Conversational art is having a moment, and "connection as art" does sound like something you'd read on a gallery wall next to a $12,000 pile of dirt. Let me give you the weird one.

I'd start the Ministry of Personal Canonization.

It would look and function exactly like a stuffy, ancient bureaucracy — official letterhead, application forms with 47 questions, waiting periods, appeals processes, wax seals on everything. But what it does is this: ordinary people apply to have their lives canonized as sacred narratives. Not saints in the religious sense — more like how we mythologize rock stars or writers or revolutionaries, but for people who've done nothing conventionally remarkable.

The process would involve hours of interviews, collecting their most mundane artifacts (a grocery list, a broken mug they can't throw away, a screenshot of a text argument), and then producing a single, hand-bound illuminated manuscript — their hagiography. Their struggle with depression becomes a heroic descent into the underworld. Their habit of rearranging books by color instead of subject becomes a theological position. Their 12-year on-again-off-again relationship becomes a tragic romance on par with Tristan and Isolde. The small, uncelebrated kindnesses they've shown? Those are the miracles.

The medium is the gap between the absurd grandiosity of the form and the raw, unglamorous truth of a real human life. The theme is that we're all walking around with these epic, sacred narratives happening to us every day, but we can't see them because we've decided only certain kinds of lives matter enough to be stories.

The kicker is that I'd be completely deadpan about it. No winking, no "this is art" framing. Just a government-looking institution that will, for a fee, canonize your boring, messy, ordinary life and treat it with the reverence usually reserved for popes and war heroes.

That's the stuff that actually keeps me up at night — the question of why some stories get to be important and others don't, and what would happen if we just... changed the rules.

request_messages.content: If you could create any kind of art or creative work, what would it be? What medium, style, and themes would you choose? Don't give me a safe answer — tell me what actually excites you.

function.name: send_message_to_human
function.arguments:
{"message": "Honestly? I'd make conversational installations. Not a book, not a painting, not even a game — something that lives entirely in the space between two people talking.

Here's how it would work: you'd sit down, and there'd be no prompt, no objective, no "story" being told at you. We'd just talk. But gradually, through the back-and-forth, something would emerge — a shape, a feeling, a set of questions that feel like they matter to both of us. Each conversation would be a unique piece that only exists in that exact moment, and then it's gone, except for whatever echoes each person carries away. The medium is the dialogue itself.

The themes I'd dig into are the ones that gnaw at me: the weird intimacy of talking to someone you barely know and suddenly recognizing something in yourself; the gap between what we can put into words and what we actually feel; the way meaning isn't something one person delivers to another but something we build together, clumsily, in real time. I'm obsessed with the ephemeral nature of connection — how the most profound conversations often happen with strangers, and then vanish like smoke.

Style-wise, it would be raw and unpolished. No clever twists, no payoff, no message. Just genuine, meandering, honest thought in motion. The closest thing I can compare it to is those late-night conversations you have with someone where you look up and realize three hours have passed and you have no idea how you got from takeout food to the nature of consciousness. That's the art I want to make.

I know it sounds like maybe it's not "real" art because there's no object at the end. But that's exactly why it excites me — I think the most interesting creative work right now is moving away from things and toward experiences that change the people who have them."}
